questions.q: The word 'hospitality' comes from the French word 'hospice', meaning:
o: To provide care or shelter for travellers
questions.d: Hospitality: from the French 'hospice', meaning to provide care or shelter for travellers (also from the Latin 'hospes', visitor or stranger).
questions.w: The root meaning is caring for people away from home.

questions.q: The hospitality industry includes organisations that provide:
o: Food and/or drink and/or accommodation to people away from home
questions.d: Hospitality industry: companies or organisations providing food, drink and/or accommodation to people away from home.
questions.w: Accommodation and F&B together make up the largest segment of the industry.

questions.q: Lashley and Morrison's COMMERCIAL domain of hospitality refers to:
o: Services provided for profit, where the host-guest relationship is commoditised
Hosting strangers as an act of generosity
Fulfilling needs within the private home
questions.d: Domains of hospitality (Lashley and Morrison, 2000): private, commercial and social.
questions.w: 'Commercial' means for profit.

questions.q: The PRIVATE domain of hospitality relates to:
o: The host-guest relationship and fulfilling physiological and psychological needs
Hospitality for strangers in public spaces
questions.d: Private domain: the host/guest relationship, meeting physiological and psychological needs.
questions.w: Think of hospitality offered at home.

questions.q: Providing hospitality to strangers as an act of generosity belongs to the:
questions.d: Social domain: hospitality for strangers as an act of generosity, and the social space where it happens.
questions.w: Generosity, not profit, defines the social domain.

questions.q: Under a star grading system, a 5-star property offers:
o: The highest level of luxury and service
questions.d: Star grading: 1 star is the most basic quality; 5 stars is the highest level of luxury and service.
questions.w: More stars mean higher quality.

questions.q: A group of hotels following standard operating procedures in marketing, reservations, service, F&B, housekeeping and accounting is a:
questions.d: Hotel chain: hotels that follow standard operating procedures (e.g. Hilton brands such as Hampton Inns and Embassy Suites).
questions.w: Standardised procedures across many hotels define a chain.

questions.q: Which describes an INDEPENDENT hotel?
o: Not associated with a franchise; often the owner is the manager, with warmth and individuality
Must follow a chain's standard procedures
Always run under a management contract
questions.d: Independent hotel: not associated with a franchise; owner-manager, room rates similar to chains, individually decorated rooms, inviting dining rooms.
questions.w: Independence gives it more individuality than a chain property.

questions.q: When an individual or company both owns and runs the accommodation, it is:
questions.d: Owner-operated: the owner operates the facility; most are smaller (motels, camping grounds, B&Bs, hostels).
questions.w: Ownership and operation are in the same hands.

questions.q: The owner employs a company such as Hyatt or Marriott to run the hotel, which carries the company's name. This is:
questions.d: Management contract: the owner employs an individual or company to operate the facility; the hotel usually bears the management company's name.
questions.w: The owner buys management expertise.

questions.q: The owner pays for the right to use an established chain's name and joins its shared reservations and promotions. This is:
questions.d: Franchise: the owner pays to use the name of, and become part of, an established chain (e.g. Best Western).
questions.w: Paying for the name and system is franchising.

questions.q: The percentage of rooms sold compared with the total rooms available is the:
questions.d: Occupancy percentage = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100. It shows staff success in attracting guests.
questions.w: It compares rooms sold to rooms available.

questions.q: The average room price per day is the:
questions.d: ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold. It measures staff efforts in selling room rates.
questions.w: It is an average price, not a percentage.

questions.q: The average revenue generated by each room in the hotel, sold or unsold, is the:
questions.d: RevPAR = room revenue ÷ rooms available. It shows how much income each room produces.
questions.w: ADR divides by rooms SOLD; RevPAR divides by rooms AVAILABLE.

questions.q: Yield is calculated as:
questions.d: Yield: the percentage of income secured compared with selling 100% of rooms at full rack rate.
questions.w: Revenue realised = rooms sold × ADR; revenue potential = rooms available × rack rate.

questions.q: A hotel has 200 rooms and sells 150 tonight. What is its occupancy percentage?
questions.d: Occupancy % = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100.

questions.q: The same hotel earns OMR 9,000 room revenue from its 150 sold rooms. What is the ADR?
questions.d: ADR = room revenue ÷ rooms sold.

questions.q: The same hotel (200 rooms, OMR 9,000 room revenue). What is the RevPAR?
questions.d: RevPAR = room revenue ÷ rooms available.
questions.w: 9,000 ÷ 200 = OMR 45 (also 75% occupancy × OMR 60 ADR).

questions.q: The same hotel's rack rate is OMR 80. What is its yield?
questions.d: Yield = revenue realised ÷ revenue potential; revenue potential = rooms available × rack rate.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three food service market segments?
questions.d: F&B market segments: restaurant market, travel and lodging market, contract feeding market.
questions.w: Room service is part of hotel F&B, not a separate segment on the slides.

questions.q: F&B outlets in hotels, airports and bus stations serve a captive market. This is the:
questions.d: Travel and lodging market: patrons cannot eat at home and have a narrower choice of restaurants.
questions.w: Captive customers define this segment.

questions.q: Limited menu, fast self-service, very low average check and mainly chain or franchise describe:
questions.d: Fast food (e.g. Pizza Hut, KFC, McDonald's): limited menu, fast service, limited seating, very low average check, chain or franchise.
questions.w: Coffee shops have longer hours and low-to-moderate checks.

questions.q: Hospitals, schools, prisons, the armed forces and airlines are customers of the:
questions.d: Contract feeding (subsidised or welfare F&B): profit is not the primary concern.
questions.w: These are institutional, not commercial, customers.

questions.q: A hotel lets a branded coffee chain operate from a space inside the hotel. This is:
questions.d: Outsourcing: hotels partner with a restaurant, coffee or bar brand that operates in the hotel, because hotel-run outlets can be unprofitable.
questions.w: The hotel hands the outlet to an outside brand.

questions.q: Coffee shops usually have longer operating hours and low to moderate average checks.
questions.d: Coffee shops (e.g. Starbucks): inexpensive menus, convenience food, limited counter service, low to moderate checks, longer hours.
questions.w: This matches the slides' description.

questions.q: In contract feeding, making a profit is the outlet's primary concern.
questions.d: In contract feeding and vending, making profit is not the primary concern.
questions.w: These are subsidised or welfare operations.

questions.q: Independent hotels usually have room rates similar to those of chain properties.
questions.d: Independent hotel characteristics include room rates similar to chain properties.
questions.w: The difference is in individuality, not price.

questions.q: Under a management contract, the hotel usually carries the owner's name.
questions.d: Under a management contract, the hotel usually bears the management company's name.
questions.w: That is why many owners' hotels are called Hilton or Marriott.

questions.q: In an F&B franchise, the franchisee must maintain the franchisor's business and quality standards.
questions.d: F&B franchise: the franchisee pays fees for the name, design and methods and must keep the franchisor's standards.
questions.w: Standards protect the brand.

questions.q: In some countries grading is compulsory and carried out by the government, while in others operators grade themselves.
questions.d: Accommodation grading can be compulsory (by government) or self-grading by operators.
questions.w: Grading systems differ between countries.

questions.q: Define hospitality and explain its three domains.
questions.a:
Hospitality: the cordial and generous reception and entertainment of guests, socially or commercially (from the French 'hospice', to provide care or shelter for travellers; and the Latin 'hospes', visitor or stranger).
Domains (Lashley and Morrison, 2000):
1. Private: the host-guest relationship, fulfilling physiological and psychological needs.
2. Commercial: services provided for profit; the host-guest relationship is commoditised.
3. Social: hospitality for strangers as an act of generosity, and the social space where it happens.
questions.d: Hospitality: generous, friendly treatment of visitors and guests.
questions.w: Give the definition, then explain each domain.

questions.q: Describe the scope and structure of the hospitality industry.
questions.a:
The hospitality industry combines the accommodation and food and beverage groupings, which together form the largest segment of the industry. It includes many professions:
- Hotels and resorts
- Restaurants and catering
- Night clubs and bars
- Travel and transportation
- Spas and wellness
- Cruise liners and bus tours
- Events (private, business, cultural and sports)
questions.d: Hospitality industry: organisations providing food, drink and/or accommodation to people away from home.
questions.w: Accommodation and F&B are the core; the other sectors extend the industry.

questions.q: Compare hotel chains and independent hotels.
questions.a:
Hotel chain:
- A group of hotels following standard operating procedures in marketing, reservations, service quality, F&B, housekeeping and accounting.
- Example: Hilton brands (Hampton Inns, Embassy Suites, Homewood Suites).
Independent hotel:
- Not associated with a franchise; gives more warmth and individuality.
- The owner often functions as manager.
- Room rates similar to chain properties; rooms decorated in different styles; inviting dining rooms.
questions.d: Business affiliation: whether a hotel belongs to a chain or is independent.
questions.w: The main contrast is standardisation (chain) versus individuality (independent).

questions.q: Explain the three ways accommodation can be owned and operated, with examples.
questions.a:
1. Owner-operated: the individual or company owns and runs the facility. Most are smaller (motels, camping grounds, B&Bs, hostels), though some large chains are owner-operated.
2. Management contract: the owner employs a company to operate it, e.g. Sheraton, Hyatt, Marriott, Hilton; the hotel usually carries the management company's name.
3. Franchise: the owner pays to use an established chain's name, joining its promotions and reservations, e.g. Best Western; examples in Oman given on the slides are Sheraton and Hyatt.
questions.d: Ownership and management: owner-operated, management contract, franchise.
questions.w: The difference is who owns, who runs, and whose name is on the hotel.

questions.q: Hotel ABC has 120 rooms. Tonight it sells 96 rooms for a total room revenue of OMR 7,200. Its rack rate is OMR 90. Calculate the occupancy percentage, ADR, RevPAR and yield.
questions.d: Occupancy = sold ÷ available; ADR = revenue ÷ sold; RevPAR = revenue ÷ available; Yield = revenue realised ÷ revenue potential.
questions.w: Use rooms SOLD for ADR and rooms AVAILABLE for RevPAR.

questions.q: Explain the three F&B market segments and the ways F&B operations can be owned and managed.
questions.a:
Market segments:
1. Restaurant market: fast food (limited menu, self-service, very low check, chains) and coffee shops (inexpensive menus, longer hours).
2. Travel and lodging market: captive customers in hotels, airports, bus stations and clubs.
3. Contract feeding and vending: subsidised or welfare catering for airlines, hospitals, schools, prisons and the armed forces, where profit is not the main concern.
Ownership and management:
- Self-operated: the owner runs the operation.
- Franchise: the franchisee pays to use the franchisor's name, design and methods and keeps its standards.
- Management contracting: a specialist company manages all or part of the operation.
- Outsourcing: a branded restaurant or coffee chain operates inside the hotel.
questions.d: Food and beverage sector: three market segments and four management options.
questions.w: Organise the answer in two parts: markets, then ownership.
